title: Contact on Ktaadn
hook: on Mount Katahdin, Thoreau is shaken by raw matter: contact, contact! (The Maine Woods)

segments.voice: Yesterday, wildness: Thoreau saying we need the tonic of wildness, places we can't fully map or tame. Where did you catch a sip of it? Day one thousand two hundred fifty-two.

Cloud, all the way down to the rocks. Thoreau is climbing a mountain in Maine, the one he spells Ktaadn and we call Katahdin, and near the top he is alone inside a gray fog so thick he can barely see the boulders under his hands. No view. No reward. He turns back. And it's on the way down, crossing a stretch of bare, burned-over ground, that something breaks open in him. The calm writer of the pond starts piling up exclamation marks, as if the sentences can't hold what he's feeling.
screen: `ALONE IN THE CLOUD.` → `NO VIEW AT THE TOP.` → `ON THE WAY DOWN, IT BREAKS OPEN.`

segments.voice: First, the ground itself. The land he crosses isn't a park or a farm or a pretty view. He calls it no man's garden: earth that nobody planted, nobody tidied, nobody owns. Matter that owes him nothing. Second, the outburst. He says the real mystery isn't some far-off spirit world. It's our ordinary life in nature, being shown matter every day and touching it: "rocks, trees, wind on our cheeks!" And then four short cries: "Contact! Contact! Who are we? where are we?" Third, the strange reversal. Just before this, he admits that his own body has become strange to him. He isn't afraid of spirits, he says. What unsettles him is bodies, solid things. For a man who wrote so much about the spirit, it's a startling turn. The ghostly felt familiar. The plain rock felt like the mystery. Fourth, why it lands on an ordinary day. It's easy to handle things for hours without meeting them: the phone, the door handle, the steering wheel, the mug. Ktaadn is Thoreau getting knocked out of that. Not a vision of something beyond the world, but the world itself, suddenly undeniable, pressing back against him. Readers hear the passage differently. Some hear terror. Some hear awe. Some hear both at once. Thoreau doesn't settle it for us. He ends with questions, and leaves them open.
screen: `NO MAN'S GARDEN.` · `ROCKS, TREES, WIND ON OUR CHEEKS.` · then, large: `CONTACT! CONTACT!` · then: `THE PLAIN ROCK AS THE MYSTERY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: contact. Yesterday was about life that isn't yours. Today is about weight. Start with your feet: feel the floor pushing back up through your heels. Then, if there's a rock, a tree, a brick wall or a wooden table near you, put your hand on it. If not, put your palm flat on the floor. Press a little. Feel the temperature, the grain, the weight that doesn't move for you. Don't describe it. Don't think about what it's made of. Let it be solid under your hand. Once, quietly, try Thoreau's questions without answering them: who are we? where are we? Then come back to your palm, and stay in contact. The bell holds the time.
Contact on Ktaadn. Thoreau, coming down a Maine mountain, overwhelmed by plain matter: rocks, trees, wind. Today's word.
Your line: contact. Today, when you pick up something heavy, a bag, a pot, a stone, feel its weight in your hand for three breaths before you move on. Day one thousand two hundred fifty-two.

howItsDone: Some readers of The Maine Woods single out the Ktaadn passage, where Thoreau, descending the mountain, is overwhelmed by raw matter and cries out for contact; some take from it a practice of touching stone, bark or soil with full attention.

fork.setup: you're Thoreau, alone near the top of the mountain, and the cloud is so thick you can't see a thing. what do you do?
options: wait for days until it clears.
turn back, and find the moment on the way down.
write that the climb was wasted.
fork.reveal: he turned back without a view. the passage people remember comes on the descent, on bare, burned-over ground.

trapdoor: what you thought: a mountain trip is about the view from the top.
what it means: Thoreau's moment comes from touching bare matter, rocks, trees, wind, not from a view.
what a scholar hears: the man who wrote so much about spirit finds the solid world the stranger thing, and ends with questions, not answers.
